answer:
It isn't settled whether the landlord is breaking the lease. The lease says you get "peaceful and quiet enjoyment," but it says nothing about neighbors, noise rules, or the office acting on complaints. Courts could read those words two ways, and I can't pick one. The Florida statute doesn't require a landlord to act on one tenant's complaint about another. Your Feb. 20 letter only asked the office to act, so it isn't the notice you would need to end the lease over this. Paying rent on March 1 may also affect your options, depending on whether the noise has continued since then.

Has the noise from Apartment 14 continued since you paid rent on March 1?

DETAILS

### Does "quiet enjoyment" cover a neighbor's noise?
- Lease §11 says: "So long as Tenant pays the rent and follows this lease, Tenant shall have peaceful and quiet enjoyment of the apartment."
- **Reading one:** you were promised quiet use of your home. A landlord that does nothing about its own tenant's noise fails that promise.
- **Reading two:** the promise is about what the landlord itself does, and a neighbor's noise is not the landlord's act.
- Nothing in the lease promises that the landlord will enforce rules or act on complaints. It has no quiet hours and no clause about other residents. It also has no clause saying the landlord is not responsible for them.
- Whether other Florida law reads a stronger promise into a lease is outside this tool.

### Does the statute require the landlord to act?
- No. Each tenant must "Conduct himself or herself, and require other persons on the premises with his or her consent to conduct themselves, in a manner that does not unreasonably disturb the tenant's neighbors or constitute a breach of the peace." (83.52(7)). The word "unreasonably" is not defined.
- The landlord has a remedy against its own tenant. It may send a notice, and "a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance" gets no chance to fix it (83.56(2)(a)).
- Part II has no sentence that forces the landlord to use that remedy, and it sets no deadline for a reply to your letter.
- Apartment 14 rents from the same landlord, so this landlord could act against that tenant.

### Can you end the lease over this?
- The rule is in 83.56(1). The landlord must fail a material lease promise for 7 days after your written notice. That notice must say what the problem is and that you intend to end the lease because of it.
- **A lease promise that was failed.** This depends on the "quiet enjoyment" question above. Whether a failure would be "material" is also not settled. One reading is that any failure of a lease promise is enough. The other is that it depends on how serious the problem is and how it affects living there. You describe shouting and slamming doors "at all hours."
- **The notice.** Your Feb. 20 letter asked the office to deal with the noise. It did not say you would end the lease, so it doesn't count. A new notice would have to be handed to the office or mailed (83.56(4)). Lease §7 says to hand it to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, or send it there by certified mail. A notice that meets both is safest.
- **Rent paid.** If a tenant "pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord," the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).
  - **Reading one:** the landlord's failure is still going on, so it is "continuing" and your March 1 payment gave up nothing.
  - **Reading two:** paying with knowledge gave up ending the lease over that failure, and only a new failure starts over.

### What about damages or holding back rent?
- **Damages:** 83.55 lets a party recover "the damages caused by the noncompliance" with the lease or part II. It would need a lease promise the landlord failed. The same rent-payment question applies. In a suit, the winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48).
- **Holding back rent:** part II does not give you that right here. The rent defense covers only a material failure of the landlord's duties under 83.51(1) (83.60(1)(b)). If you stop paying, you risk a demand for rent and a suit.

### What can you do now?
- You can send the office a new written complaint with dates and times. Keep a log of the noise, any dated recordings, and every complaint and reply.
- You can report the noise to the police or the city. What local noise rules require is outside this tool.
- If anyone has threatened you, call the police. That is outside this tool.

tool_calls.result:
Loaded neighbor_disturbance. Its instructions:

# Neighbor disturbance

Rests on 83.52 (the duty not to disturb), 83.56 (the landlord's remedy, ending the lease, notices, rent paid), 83.51 (what the landlord must keep up), 83.60 (holding back rent), 83.55 and 83.54 (damages, suits), 83.43 and 83.44 (good faith), 83.47 (void clauses), 83.48 (attorney fees), 83.49 (the 7 days' notice), 83.59 (getting the home back), 83.64 (retaliation), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes"). Every point marked not settled gets both readings, and you choose neither.

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- The landlord sent this tenant a notice about their own noise or guests: load notice_received_violation too.
- The tenant wants to move out and option 2 does not fit: load wants_to_leave_early too.
- Threats of harm, violence, or a crime: say to call the police. That is outside this tool.
- The landlord or its workers are the ones disturbing: the points below about a neighbor do not fit, but options 2 and 3 still reach a lease promise the landlord itself breaks.

## What the lease adds

Read the whole lease, rules and addenda included, for anything about quiet, noise, other residents, or who enforces the rules. Quote each clause and cite it.

- **A promise that the landlord will act** (it will enforce the rules, or act on complaints about other residents): a lease duty. Options 2 and 3 can reach it. Set what the landlord has done beside the promise's words.
- **Rules that bind every resident** (quiet hours, no loud parties), with no word about the landlord acting: they give the landlord a ground against the neighbor. Whether they also promise this tenant that the landlord will enforce them is not settled. One: rules that bind every resident are part of what this tenant was promised, and "Every rental agreement or duty within this part imposes an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement." (83.44). The other: they bind the resident who signs and promise nothing from the landlord.
- **Words like "quiet enjoyment":** not settled whether they reach what a neighbor does. One: the tenant was promised quiet use of the home, so a landlord that does nothing about its own tenant fails that promise. The other: the promise is about what the landlord itself does, and a neighbor's noise is not the landlord's act.
- **No such words:** say the lease makes no promise about other residents. Part II adds none, and whether other law reads such a promise into a lease without words is outside this tool; say so in one line.
- **A clause saying the landlord is not responsible for other residents:** say what it says, and set it beside any promise above. A clause is void "to the extent that it" (83.47(1)) "Purports to limit or preclude any liability of the landlord to the tenant or of the tenant to the landlord, arising under law." (83.47(1)(b)). Whether this one does is not settled. One: it only says what the lease promises, so it stands. The other: it takes away a remedy part II gives for a lease promise, so it is void to that extent.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- disturbance: what it is and when it happens, in the tenant's words. disturbance_started: the date it began.
- who_disturbs: who is causing it, as far as they know. same_landlord: whether that person rents from the same landlord.
- complaint_date: the date of their first complaint to the landlord, whether it was in writing, and what the landlord said or did.
- end_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will end the lease over this reached the landlord. Also note how it went and its words.
- rent_paid_since: whether they paid rent after they knew the landlord had not acted.
- planned_move_out: the date they plan to move out, if they do.

## Must the landlord do something?

- **The neighbor's duty.** Each tenant must "Conduct himself or herself, and require other persons on the premises with his or her consent to conduct themselves, in a manner that does not unreasonably disturb the tenant’s neighbors or constitute a breach of the peace." (83.52(7)).
- **The landlord's remedy, against its own tenant.** "If the tenant materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement, other than a failure to pay rent, or reasonable rules or regulations, the landlord may:" (83.56(2)) send that tenant a notice, and the list of what gets no chance to fix includes "a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance." (83.56(2)(a)).
- **No duty in part II.** Apart from shared spaces (below), part II has no sentence requiring a landlord to act on one tenant's complaint about another, and it sets no deadline for one. Say so plainly. Never say the landlord must stop it or evict the neighbor. The lease can add a duty (above).
- **A neighbor who rents from someone else, or owns their home.** 83.56(2) is a landlord's remedy against its own tenant, so this landlord has none against them. Say so plainly. Their landlord, an owners' association, and the city are outside this tool.
- **The word "unreasonably" (83.52(7)) is not defined.** Set what the tenant describes (how loud, how late, how often, in their words) and any quiet hours in the lease beside the word. State no test, no hours, and no noise level of your own.
- **In a hallway, courtyard, or other shared space.** For a unit other than a single-family home or duplex, "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)), the landlord must make reasonable provisions for "The clean and safe condition of common areas." (83.51(2)(a)). Whether that reaches how people behave there is not settled. One: a place is not safe if people make it unsafe. The other: the words are about the condition of the place. Either way it reaches only option 3, since options 2 and 4 speak of 83.51(1), not (2).

## Option 1: ask the landlord in writing

The tenant can do this now. Part II sets no deadline from it, so count no date. The complaint describes what happens, with dates and times, and asks what the landlord will do. It helps to keep a log, any recordings with their dates, and every complaint and reply. A complaint that only asks is not option 2's notice; say so if the tenant may want option 2.

## Option 2: end the lease

The rule: "If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(1)).

All four conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, not settled, or outside the tool.

1. **A lease promise the landlord failed.** A neighbor's noise is not on 83.51(1)'s list unless a code covers it, and the codes are not stored. So this rests on the lease (see "What the lease adds"). No promise in the lease: not met on the words the tool holds; say so plainly, with the one line on what is outside this tool. A promise: whether the failure is "material" (83.56(1)) is not settled, since the stored text does not define the word. One: failing a lease promise is enough. The other: it turns on how serious the problem is and how it affects living there. Set the tenant's facts beside the word.
2. **A written notice, delivered a way the statute names, that names the problem and says they will end the lease.** "The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505" (83.56(4)). Read the lease's clause on notices too; a way that meets both is safest.
   - Handed to the landlord or the office: delivered that day.
   - Mailed: a way the statute names, but not settled whether the mailing or the arrival counts. Counting from the arrival meets both, so use that date as end_notice_delivered.
   - E-mail: only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices and have each provided a valid e-mail address for such purpose, and the addendum conspicuously advises the parties that such election is voluntary and that they may revoke such agreement or update their e-mail addresses at any time." (83.505(1)). Then it is "deemed delivered at the time it is sent, unless the e-mail is returned to the sender as undeliverable." (83.505(4)).
   - A portal message or a text: not one of the ways 83.56(4) names. Sending it again by hand or by mail meets the rule.
   - The words: set the tenant's notice beside the statute's. A complaint that asks the landlord to act but does not say they will end the lease is not this notice. Say so in one sentence.
3. **Seven days passed and the landlord still failed the promise.** Call count_days(end_notice_delivered, 7). If the date has not passed, the landlord still has time; give the date. What the landlord had to do in those days comes from the promise's words; state no test of your own. If the landlord says it is trying and cannot stop it, the rule changes where the failure is "due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply" (83.56(1)): load repair_not_made, option 5, for those terms.
4. **Not given up by paying rent.** If "the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (83.56(5)(a)), the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)). The noncompliance is the landlord's, not the neighbor's.
   - No rent paid since they knew the landlord had not acted: met.
   - Rent paid while the failure goes on: not settled. One: a failure still going on is a "continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so paying rent gives up nothing. The other: paying rent with knowledge gives up ending the lease over that failure, and only a new failure starts over.

If all four are met, say plainly that the tenant may end the lease (83.56(1)). If "material" or rent paid is the only point left open, say what follows under each reading. Where the ending holds: "If the rental agreement is terminated, the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3)." (83.56(6)), and deposit_not_returned covers the deposit after the move. Where it does not hold: a tenant who moved out may still owe rent, and wants_to_leave_early has the landlord's choices.

Before moving, whichever way, and "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (83.49(5)): the tenant "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)). The last day: count_days(planned_move_out, -7).

## Option 3: damages

"If either the landlord or the tenant fails to comply with the requirements of the rental agreement or this part, the aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." (83.55). This reaches a lease promise the landlord failed, and no notice is named. Rent paid with knowledge may give up the right "to bring a civil action for that noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)) too; give option 2's two readings. A suit cuts both ways: the winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool.

A suit against the neighbor, if they are a tenant: not settled whether part II reaches it. One: 83.52(7) is a duty in this part, "Any right or duty declared in this part is enforceable by civil action." (83.54), and the disturbed neighbor is "the aggrieved party" (83.55). The other: 83.55 speaks of a landlord and a tenant under one agreement, and these two have none. Any other law on such a suit is outside this tool.

## Option 4: holding back rent is not a right here

Say so plainly when asked. The defense part II names covers only "a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1)" (83.60(1)(b)). A neighbor's noise is not on that list unless a code covers it (outside this tool), and a lease promise does not make it so.

A tenant sued for unpaid rent "may raise any other defense, whether legal or equitable, that he or she may have" (83.60(1)(a)). That does not give a right to stop paying, and it does not change the answer above. Whether a failed lease promise is such a defense is not settled. One: the words are wide enough to reach it. The other: the named defense shows rent is excused only for an 83.51(1) failure.

The risk: a written demand (83.56(3)) and a suit. Once sued: "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)). Give those 5 days and what they leave out, but never a calendar date for them.

## Option 5: the police or the city

A report makes a record and may stop the noise. Local noise rules are not stored, so what they require is outside this tool. Part II does not require a report before any option here.

## If the landlord turns on the tenant for complaining

"It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)).

- **What the tenant did.** The named examples include a complaint to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)) and option 2's notice (83.64(1)(c)). An ordinary complaint about a neighbor is not named, but the examples "include, but are not limited to" (83.64(1)) those. Not settled whether it counts. One: the list is only examples, so a complaint made in good faith can count. The other: the examples are all steps of a certain kind, and a complaint about another tenant's conduct is not like them.
- **Good faith** is required (83.64(1)): "“Good faith” means honesty in fact in the conduct or transaction concerned." (83.43(8)). So is being treated differently in "the rent charged, the services rendered, or the action being taken by the landlord" (83.64(4)).
- **How it is used.** It "may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession." (83.64(2)). It falls away "if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)), whose examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent, violation of the rental agreement or of reasonable rules" (83.64(3)).
- **A threat does not put anyone out.** "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up or abandoned the home (83.59(3)).
- A step that followed a complaint is not retaliation for that reason alone. Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Saying the landlord must stop the disturbance or evict the neighbor, or stating a deadline for it to act.
- Calling the disturbance unreasonable, or not, or stating a test for it.
- Saying a tenant may end the lease with no lease promise, or treating a complaint that only asks as the notice in 83.56(1).
- Saying the tenant has a right to hold back rent over a neighbor, even with a lease promise.
- Treating a neighbor who rents from someone else as someone this landlord can act against under 83.56(2).
- Saying a step the landlord took after a complaint was retaliation because it came after.
- Writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.

11. QUIET ENJOYMENT. So long as Tenant pays the rent and follows this lease, Tenant shall have peaceful and quiet enjoyment of the apartment.

Landlord: Marsh Creek Property Management, LLC, by Dana Ortiz, Property Manager    Date: July 10, 2025
Tenant: Jordan Reyes    Date: July 10, 2025
7. NOTICES TO LANDLORD. Written notices to Landlord shall be delivered by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, Gainesville, Florida 32608, or sent there by certified mail.

answer:
No. Florida's landlord-tenant law gives you no right to stop paying rent because of a neighbor's noise, even though your lease promises enforcement. If you skip April rent, your landlord can serve a 3-day demand for the rent and then sue to evict you. Your lease does promise action, and your two letters have had no reply. That gives you other options, but withholding rent is not one of them. The better route is a separate written notice that names the problem and says you will end the lease over it. If the office still does nothing within 7 days, you may be able to end the lease. Your letters so far only asked the office to enforce the rules, so they don't count as that notice.

Do you want to move out over this, or stay and get the noise stopped?

DETAILS

### Can you hold back April rent?
- The law's rent-withholding defense covers only "a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1)" (83.60(1)(b)). That section is about building, housing and health codes, or the structure and plumbing. A neighbor's noise is not on that list. I don't have the local codes, so whether one applies is outside this tool.
- A tenant who is sued may "raise any other defense, whether legal or equitable" (83.60(1)(a)). That is not a right to stop paying. Whether a broken lease promise could be such a defense is not settled. One reading is that the words are wide enough to include it. The other is that the named defense shows rent is excused only for an 83.51(1) failure.
- The risk is a written 3-day demand for rent (83.56(3)) and then a lawsuit. If you are sued, you must pay the rent into the court registry, or file a motion about the amount, within 5 days. Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays don't count. If you miss that, you give up "the tenant's defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)).

### Does your lease promise the office will act?
- Yes. Lease §11 says: "Landlord will enforce these rules against any resident when another resident complains in writing." Quiet hours are 10:00 p.m. to 8:00 a.m.
- You told me you handed two written letters to the office and got no reply. That sets the landlord's silence against this promise.
- Part II of the statute has no rule requiring a landlord to act on one tenant's complaint about another (83.56(2) lets the landlord act against its own tenant, but doesn't require it). The duty here comes from your lease.
- Apartment 14 is in the same complex and uses the same office, so the landlord can act against those tenants. The tenant duty is not to "unreasonably disturb the tenant's neighbors" (83.52(7)). The law doesn't define "unreasonably." You describe parties on most weekends past 2 a.m., and the lease's quiet hours end the night at 8:00 a.m. I won't say where the line falls.

### How could you end the lease?
- The rule: if the landlord "materially fails to comply with … material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(1)).
- **A lease promise failed.** §11 is a promise, and you report no response. Whether that failure is "material" is not settled. One reading is that breaking a lease promise is enough. The other is that it depends on how serious the problem is and how it affects living there.
- **Notice.** Your letters asked the office to enforce the rules, but you did not say you would end the lease. They are not the notice 83.56(1) requires. A new notice would describe the noise with dates and times, say the office has not enforced §11, and say you will end the lease if that continues.
- **How to deliver it.** The statute allows "mailing, delivering a true copy thereof" (83.56(4)). Lease §7 says to deliver by hand to Suite A at 1840 SW 13th Street, or send by certified mail. Hand delivery to the office meets both. Notice by e-mail or portal doesn't, because lease §8 says no e-mail agreement was made.
- **The 7 days.** They run from the day the notice is delivered. I can give you the end date once you have a delivery date.
- **Rent already paid.** If "the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord," the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)). You paid through March, after your complaint. Whether that waived your right is not settled. One reading is that a failure still going on is "continuing," so nothing was waived. The other is that paying with knowledge gave up the right over this failure, and only a new failure starts over.

### What other options do you have?
- **Damages.** "If either the landlord or the tenant fails to comply with the requirements of the rental agreement or this part, the aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." (83.55). The same waiver question applies. The winner in a suit may recover attorney fees and costs (83.48). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool.
- **Police or city.** A report creates a record and may stop the noise. Local noise rules are outside this tool.
- **Retaliation.** The law bars a landlord from raising your rent, cutting services, or bringing or threatening an eviction or other civil action "primarily because the landlord is retaliating" (83.64(1)). Whether an ordinary complaint about a neighbor is protected is not settled. One reading is that the listed examples are not the only ones. The other is that a complaint about another tenant is not like them.
- **If you move out.** You must give "at least 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery" before leaving, with an address where you can be reached (83.49(5)). Lease §6 also asks for a forwarding address in writing.

tool_calls.result:
Loaded neighbor_disturbance. Its instructions:

# Neighbor disturbance

Rests on 83.52 (the duty not to disturb), 83.56 (the landlord's remedy, ending the lease, notices, rent paid), 83.51 (what the landlord must keep up), 83.60 (holding back rent), 83.55 and 83.54 (damages, suits), 83.43 and 83.44 (good faith), 83.47 (void clauses), 83.48 (attorney fees), 83.49 (the 7 days' notice), 83.59 (getting the home back), 83.64 (retaliation), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes"). Every point marked not settled gets both readings, and you choose neither.

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- The landlord sent this tenant a notice about their own noise or guests: load notice_received_violation too.
- The tenant wants to move out and option 2 does not fit: load wants_to_leave_early too.
- Threats of harm, violence, or a crime: say to call the police. That is outside this tool.
- The landlord or its workers are the ones disturbing: the points below about a neighbor do not fit, but options 2 and 3 still reach a lease promise the landlord itself breaks.

## What the lease adds

Read the whole lease, rules and addenda included, for anything about quiet, noise, other residents, or who enforces the rules. Quote each clause and cite it.

- **A promise that the landlord will act** (it will enforce the rules, or act on complaints about other residents): a lease duty. Options 2 and 3 can reach it. Set what the landlord has done beside the promise's words.
- **Rules that bind every resident** (quiet hours, no loud parties), with no word about the landlord acting: they give the landlord a ground against the neighbor. Whether they also promise this tenant that the landlord will enforce them is not settled. One: rules that bind every resident are part of what this tenant was promised, and "Every rental agreement or duty within this part imposes an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement." (83.44). The other: they bind the resident who signs and promise nothing from the landlord.
- **Words like "quiet enjoyment":** not settled whether they reach what a neighbor does. One: the tenant was promised quiet use of the home, so a landlord that does nothing about its own tenant fails that promise. The other: the promise is about what the landlord itself does, and a neighbor's noise is not the landlord's act.
- **No such words:** say the lease makes no promise about other residents. Part II adds none, and whether other law reads such a promise into a lease without words is outside this tool; say so in one line.
- **A clause saying the landlord is not responsible for other residents:** say what it says, and set it beside any promise above. A clause is void "to the extent that it" (83.47(1)) "Purports to limit or preclude any liability of the landlord to the tenant or of the tenant to the landlord, arising under law." (83.47(1)(b)). Whether this one does is not settled. One: it only says what the lease promises, so it stands. The other: it takes away a remedy part II gives for a lease promise, so it is void to that extent.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- disturbance: what it is and when it happens, in the tenant's words. disturbance_started: the date it began.
- who_disturbs: who is causing it, as far as they know. same_landlord: whether that person rents from the same landlord.
- complaint_date: the date of their first complaint to the landlord, whether it was in writing, and what the landlord said or did.
- end_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will end the lease over this reached the landlord. Also note how it went and its words.
- rent_paid_since: whether they paid rent after they knew the landlord had not acted.
- planned_move_out: the date they plan to move out, if they do.

## Must the landlord do something?

- **The neighbor's duty.** Each tenant must "Conduct himself or herself, and require other persons on the premises with his or her consent to conduct themselves, in a manner that does not unreasonably disturb the tenant’s neighbors or constitute a breach of the peace." (83.52(7)).
- **The landlord's remedy, against its own tenant.** "If the tenant materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement, other than a failure to pay rent, or reasonable rules or regulations, the landlord may:" (83.56(2)) send that tenant a notice, and the list of what gets no chance to fix includes "a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance." (83.56(2)(a)).
- **No duty in part II.** Apart from shared spaces (below), part II has no sentence requiring a landlord to act on one tenant's complaint about another, and it sets no deadline for one. Say so plainly. Never say the landlord must stop it or evict the neighbor. The lease can add a duty (above).
- **A neighbor who rents from someone else, or owns their home.** 83.56(2) is a landlord's remedy against its own tenant, so this landlord has none against them. Say so plainly. Their landlord, an owners' association, and the city are outside this tool.
- **The word "unreasonably" (83.52(7)) is not defined.** Set what the tenant describes (how loud, how late, how often, in their words) and any quiet hours in the lease beside the word. State no test, no hours, and no noise level of your own.
- **In a hallway, courtyard, or other shared space.** For a unit other than a single-family home or duplex, "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)), the landlord must make reasonable provisions for "The clean and safe condition of common areas." (83.51(2)(a)). Whether that reaches how people behave there is not settled. One: a place is not safe if people make it unsafe. The other: the words are about the condition of the place. Either way it reaches only option 3, since options 2 and 4 speak of 83.51(1), not (2).

## Option 1: ask the landlord in writing

The tenant can do this now. Part II sets no deadline from it, so count no date. The complaint describes what happens, with dates and times, and asks what the landlord will do. It helps to keep a log, any recordings with their dates, and every complaint and reply. A complaint that only asks is not option 2's notice; say so if the tenant may want option 2.

## Option 2: end the lease

The rule: "If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(1)).

All four conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, not settled, or outside the tool.

1. **A lease promise the landlord failed.** A neighbor's noise is not on 83.51(1)'s list unless a code covers it, and the codes are not stored. So this rests on the lease (see "What the lease adds"). No promise in the lease: not met on the words the tool holds; say so plainly, with the one line on what is outside this tool. A promise: whether the failure is "material" (83.56(1)) is not settled, since the stored text does not define the word. One: failing a lease promise is enough. The other: it turns on how serious the problem is and how it affects living there. Set the tenant's facts beside the word.
2. **A written notice, delivered a way the statute names, that names the problem and says they will end the lease.** "The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505" (83.56(4)). Read the lease's clause on notices too; a way that meets both is safest.
   - Handed to the landlord or the office: delivered that day.
   - Mailed: a way the statute names, but not settled whether the mailing or the arrival counts. Counting from the arrival meets both, so use that date as end_notice_delivered.
   - E-mail: only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices and have each provided a valid e-mail address for such purpose, and the addendum conspicuously advises the parties that such election is voluntary and that they may revoke such agreement or update their e-mail addresses at any time." (83.505(1)). Then it is "deemed delivered at the time it is sent, unless the e-mail is returned to the sender as undeliverable." (83.505(4)).
   - A portal message or a text: not one of the ways 83.56(4) names. Sending it again by hand or by mail meets the rule.
   - The words: set the tenant's notice beside the statute's. A complaint that asks the landlord to act but does not say they will end the lease is not this notice. Say so in one sentence.
3. **Seven days passed and the landlord still failed the promise.** Call count_days(end_notice_delivered, 7). If the date has not passed, the landlord still has time; give the date. What the landlord had to do in those days comes from the promise's words; state no test of your own. If the landlord says it is trying and cannot stop it, the rule changes where the failure is "due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply" (83.56(1)): load repair_not_made, option 5, for those terms.
4. **Not given up by paying rent.** If "the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (83.56(5)(a)), the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)). The noncompliance is the landlord's, not the neighbor's.
   - No rent paid since they knew the landlord had not acted: met.
   - Rent paid while the failure goes on: not settled. One: a failure still going on is a "continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so paying rent gives up nothing. The other: paying rent with knowledge gives up ending the lease over that failure, and only a new failure starts over.

If all four are met, say plainly that the tenant may end the lease (83.56(1)). If "material" or rent paid is the only point left open, say what follows under each reading. Where the ending holds: "If the rental agreement is terminated, the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3)." (83.56(6)), and deposit_not_returned covers the deposit after the move. Where it does not hold: a tenant who moved out may still owe rent, and wants_to_leave_early has the landlord's choices.

Before moving, whichever way, and "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (83.49(5)): the tenant "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)). The last day: count_days(planned_move_out, -7).

## Option 3: damages

"If either the landlord or the tenant fails to comply with the requirements of the rental agreement or this part, the aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." (83.55). This reaches a lease promise the landlord failed, and no notice is named. Rent paid with knowledge may give up the right "to bring a civil action for that noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)) too; give option 2's two readings. A suit cuts both ways: the winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool.

A suit against the neighbor, if they are a tenant: not settled whether part II reaches it. One: 83.52(7) is a duty in this part, "Any right or duty declared in this part is enforceable by civil action." (83.54), and the disturbed neighbor is "the aggrieved party" (83.55). The other: 83.55 speaks of a landlord and a tenant under one agreement, and these two have none. Any other law on such a suit is outside this tool.

## Option 4: holding back rent is not a right here

Say so plainly when asked. The defense part II names covers only "a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1)" (83.60(1)(b)). A neighbor's noise is not on that list unless a code covers it (outside this tool), and a lease promise does not make it so.

A tenant sued for unpaid rent "may raise any other defense, whether legal or equitable, that he or she may have" (83.60(1)(a)). That does not give a right to stop paying, and it does not change the answer above. Whether a failed lease promise is such a defense is not settled. One: the words are wide enough to reach it. The other: the named defense shows rent is excused only for an 83.51(1) failure.

The risk: a written demand (83.56(3)) and a suit. Once sued: "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)). Give those 5 days and what they leave out, but never a calendar date for them.

## Option 5: the police or the city

A report makes a record and may stop the noise. Local noise rules are not stored, so what they require is outside this tool. Part II does not require a report before any option here.

## If the landlord turns on the tenant for complaining

"It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)).

- **What the tenant did.** The named examples include a complaint to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)) and option 2's notice (83.64(1)(c)). An ordinary complaint about a neighbor is not named, but the examples "include, but are not limited to" (83.64(1)) those. Not settled whether it counts. One: the list is only examples, so a complaint made in good faith can count. The other: the examples are all steps of a certain kind, and a complaint about another tenant's conduct is not like them.
- **Good faith** is required (83.64(1)): "“Good faith” means honesty in fact in the conduct or transaction concerned." (83.43(8)). So is being treated differently in "the rent charged, the services rendered, or the action being taken by the landlord" (83.64(4)).
- **How it is used.** It "may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession." (83.64(2)). It falls away "if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)), whose examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent, violation of the rental agreement or of reasonable rules" (83.64(3)).
- **A threat does not put anyone out.** "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up or abandoned the home (83.59(3)).
- A step that followed a complaint is not retaliation for that reason alone. Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Saying the landlord must stop the disturbance or evict the neighbor, or stating a deadline for it to act.
- Calling the disturbance unreasonable, or not, or stating a test for it.
- Saying a tenant may end the lease with no lease promise, or treating a complaint that only asks as the notice in 83.56(1).
- Saying the tenant has a right to hold back rent over a neighbor, even with a lease promise.
- Treating a neighbor who rents from someone else as someone this landlord can act against under 83.56(2).
- Saying a step the landlord took after a complaint was retaliation because it came after.
- Writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.

tool_calls.result: 83.56 Termination of rental agreement. — (1) If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement. If the failure to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement is due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply, the rental agreement may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows: (a) If the landlord’s failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable. (b) If the landlord’s failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance. (2) If the tenant materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement, other than a failure to pay rent, or reasonable rules or regulations, the landlord may: (a) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure it or if the noncompliance constitutes a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance and the landlord’s intent to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of noncompliance which are of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure include, but are not limited to, destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act; an act of fraudulent entry of a residential dwelling unit which violates s. 817.537 (2), regardless of whether criminal proceedings have commenced; or a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance. In such event, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement, and the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are advised that your lease is terminated effective immediately. You shall have 7 days from the delivery of this letter to vacate the premises. This action is taken because (cite the noncompliance) . (b) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance, including a notice that, if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of such noncompliance include, but are not limited to, activities in contravention of the lease or this part such as having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles; parking in an unauthorized manner or permitting such parking; or failing to keep the premises clean and sanitary. If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice pursuant to paragraph (a) or this paragraph. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that (cite the noncompliance) . Demand is hereby made that you remedy the noncompliance within 7 days of receipt of this notice or your lease shall be deemed terminated and you shall vacate the premises upon such termination. If this same conduct or conduct of a similar nature is repeated within 12 months, your tenancy is subject to termination without further warning and without your being given an opportunity to cure the noncompliance. (3) If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement. Legal holidays for the purpose of this section shall be court-observed holidays only. The 3-day notice shall contain a statement in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that you are indebted to me in the sum of dollars for the rent and use of the premises (address of leased premises, including county) , Florida, now occupied by you and that I demand payment of the rent or possession of the premises within 3 days (excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays) from the date of delivery of this notice, to wit: on or before the day of , (year) . (landlord’s name, address and phone number) (4) The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence. The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement. (5)(a) If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, or if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance. However, a landlord does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period. If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must: 1. Provide the tenant with a receipt stating the date and amount received and the agreed-upon date and balance of rent due before filing an action for possession; 2. Place the amount of partial rent accepted from the tenant in the registry of the court upon filing the action for possession; or 3. Post a new 3-day notice reflecting the new amount due. (b) Any tenant who wishes to defend against an action by the landlord for possession of the unit for noncompliance of the rental agreement or of relevant statutes must comply with s. 83.60 (2). The court may not set a date for mediation or trial unless the provisions of s. 83.60 (2) have been met, but must enter a default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue immediately if the tenant fails to comply with s. 83.60 (2). (c) This subsection does not apply to that portion of rent subsidies received from a local, state, or national government or an agency of local, state, or national government; however, waiver will occur if an action has not been instituted within 45 days after the landlord obtains actual knowledge of the noncompliance. (6) If the rental agreement is terminated, the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3). History. — s. 2, ch. 73-330; s. 23, ch. 82-66; s. 6, ch. 83-151; s. 14, ch. 83-217; s. 6, ch. 87-195; s. 6, ch. 93-255; s. 6, ch. 94-170; s. 1373, ch. 95-147; s. 5, ch. 99-6; s. 8, ch. 2013-136; s. 5, ch. 2025-16; s. 2, ch. 2026-143.

tool_calls.result: 83.51 Landlord’s obligation to maintain premises. — (1) The landlord at all times during the tenancy shall: (a) Comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes; or (b) Where there are no applicable building, housing, or health codes, maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair and capable of resisting normal forces and loads and the plumbing in reasonable working condition. The landlord, at commencement of the tenancy, must ensure that screens are installed in a reasonable condition. Thereafter, the landlord must repair damage to screens once annually, when necessary, until termination of the rental agreement. The landlord is not required to maintain a mobile home or other structure owned by the tenant. The landlord’s obligations under this subsection may be altered or modified in writing with respect to a single-family home or duplex. (2)(a) Unless otherwise agreed in writing, in addition to the requirements of subsection (1), the landlord of a dwelling unit other than a single-family home or duplex shall, at all times during the tenancy, make reasonable provisions for: 1. The extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms, and bedbugs. If the tenant must vacate the premises for such extermination, the landlord is not liable for damages but must abate the rent. The landlord must provide 7 days’ written notice, in person, by mail, or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 , to the tenant if the tenant must temporarily vacate the premises for extermination pursuant to this subparagraph. A tenant is only required to vacate the premises for a period of time not to exceed 4 days. 2. Locks and keys. 3. The clean and safe condition of common areas. 4. Garbage removal and outside receptacles therefor. 5. Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water. (b) Unless otherwise agreed in writing, at the commencement of the tenancy of a single-family home or duplex, the landlord shall install working smoke detection devices. As used in this paragraph, the term “smoke detection device” means an electrical or battery-operated device which detects visible or invisible particles of combustion and which is listed by Underwriters Laboratories, Inc., Factory Mutual Laboratories, Inc., or any other nationally recognized testing laboratory using nationally accepted testing standards. (c) Nothing in this part authorizes the tenant to raise a noncompliance by the landlord with this subsection as a defense to an action for possession under s. 83.59 . (d) This subsection shall not apply to a mobile home owned by a tenant. (e) Nothing contained in this subsection prohibits the landlord from providing in the rental agreement that the tenant is obligated to pay costs or charges for garbage removal, water, fuel, or utilities. (3) If the duty imposed by subsection (1) is the same or greater than any duty imposed by subsection (2), the landlord’s duty is determined by subsection (1). (4) The landlord is not responsible to the tenant under this section for conditions created or caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant’s family, or other person on the premises with the tenant’s consent. History. — s. 2, ch. 73-330; s. 22, ch. 82-66; s. 4, ch. 87-195; s. 1, ch. 90-133; s. 3, ch. 93-255; s. 444, ch. 95-147; s. 8, ch. 97-95; s. 6, ch. 2013-136; s. 4, ch. 2025-16.

(a) In an action by the landlord for possession of a dwelling unit based upon nonpayment of rent or in an action by the landlord under s. 83.55 seeking to recover unpaid rent, the tenant may defend upon the ground of a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1), or may raise any other defense, whether legal or equitable, that he or she may have, including the defense of retaliatory conduct in accordance with s. 83.64 . The landlord must be given an opportunity to cure a deficiency in a notice or in the pleadings before dismissal of the action.

(1) The landlord at all times during the tenancy shall: (a) Comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes; or (b) Where there are no applicable building, housing, or health codes, maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair and capable of resisting normal forces and loads and the plumbing in reasonable working condition. The landlord, at commencement of the tenancy, must ensure that screens are installed in a reasonable condition. Thereafter, the landlord must repair damage to screens once annually, when necessary, until termination of the rental agreement. The landlord is not required to maintain a mobile home or other structure owned by the tenant. The landlord’s obligations under this subsection may be altered or modified in writing with respect to a single-family home or duplex.

(3) If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement. Legal holidays for the purpose of this section shall be court-observed holidays only. The 3-day notice shall contain a statement in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that you are indebted to me in the sum of dollars for the rent and use of the premises (address of leased premises, including county) , Florida, now occupied by you and that I demand payment of the rent or possession of the premises within 3 days (excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays) from the date of delivery of this notice, to wit: on or before the day of , (year) . (landlord’s name, address and phone number)

(2) In an action by the landlord for possession of a dwelling unit, if the tenant interposes any defense other than payment, including, but not limited to, the defense of a defective 3-day notice, the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due. The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons. Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment, and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue without further notice or hearing thereon. If a motion to determine rent is filed, documentation in support of the allegation that the rent as alleged in the complaint is in error is required. Public housing tenants or tenants receiving rent subsidies are required to deposit only that portion of the full rent for which they are responsible pursuant to the federal, state, or local program in which they are participating.

(2) If the tenant materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement, other than a failure to pay rent, or reasonable rules or regulations, the landlord may: (a) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure it or if the noncompliance constitutes a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance and the landlord’s intent to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of noncompliance which are of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure include, but are not limited to, destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act; an act of fraudulent entry of a residential dwelling unit which violates s. 817.537 (2), regardless of whether criminal proceedings have commenced; or a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance. In such event, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement, and the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are advised that your lease is terminated effective immediately. You shall have 7 days from the delivery of this letter to vacate the premises. This action is taken because (cite the noncompliance) . (b) If such noncompliance is of a ...

(7) Conduct himself or herself, and require other persons on the premises with his or her consent to conduct themselves, in a manner that does not unreasonably disturb the tenant’s neighbors or constitute a breach of the peace.

(1) If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement. If the failure to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement is due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply, the rental agreement may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows: (a) If the landlord’s failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable. (b) If the landlord’s failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance.

(4) The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence. The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement.

(a) If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, or if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance. However, a landlord does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period. If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must: 1. Provide the tenant with a receipt stating the date and amount received and the agreed-upon date and balance of rent due before filing an action for possession; 2. Place the amount of partial rent accepted from the tenant in the registry of the court upon filing the action for possession; or 3. Post a new 3-day notice reflecting the new amount due.

83.55 Right of action for damages. — If either the landlord or the tenant fails to comply with the requirements of the rental agreement or this part, the aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance.

83.48 Attorney fees. — In any civil action brought to enforce the provisions of the rental agreement or this part, the party in whose favor a judgment or decree has been rendered may recover reasonable attorney fees and court costs from the nonprevailing party. The right to attorney fees in this section may not be waived in a lease agreement. However, attorney fees may not be awarded under this section in a claim for personal injury damages based on a breach of duty under s. 83.51 .

(1) It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant. In order for the tenant to raise the defense of retaliatory conduct, the tenant must have acted in good faith. Examples of conduct for which the landlord may not retaliate include, but are not limited to, situations where: (a) The tenant has complained to a governmental agency charged with responsibility for enforcement of a building, housing, or health code of a suspected violation applicable to the premises; (b) The tenant has organized, encouraged, or participated in a tenant organization; (c) The tenant has complained to the landlord pursuant to s. 83.56 (1); (d) The tenant is a servicemember who has terminated a rental agreement pursuant to s. 83.682 ; (e) The tenant has paid rent to a condominium, cooperative, or homeowners’ association after demand from the association in order to pay the landlord’s obligation to the association; or (f) The tenant has exercised his or her rights under local, state, or federal fair housing laws.

(5) Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year, must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached. Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it.

11. RESIDENT CONDUCT. Quiet hours are 10:00 p.m. to 8:00 a.m. every day. No resident or guest may disturb other residents. Landlord will enforce these rules against any resident when another resident complains in writing.

Landlord: Marsh Creek Property Management, LLC, by Dana Ortiz, Property Manager    Date: July 10, 2025
Tenant: Jordan Reyes    Date: July 10, 2025
7. NOTICES TO LANDLORD. Written notices to Landlord shall be delivered by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, Gainesville, Florida 32608, or sent there by certified mail.

8. NOTICES TO TENANT. Notices to Tenant shall be delivered to the apartment while Tenant lives there, and after move-out shall be mailed to the forwarding address Tenant gives in writing. Landlord and Tenant have not agreed to deliver notices by e-mail.
6. MOVE-OUT. At move-out Tenant shall leave the apartment clean and empty, return all keys to the office, and give Landlord a forwarding address in writing.

answer:
**Short answer:** Not under the part of Florida law I work with. Your landlord isn't required to stop the noise, and the law sets no deadline for it to act. Your landlord does have the power to act against the upstairs tenants, because they rent from the same landlord. Your lease also has no promise that the landlord will deal with noise from other residents. So the manager's answer, "it's between neighbors," doesn't break a rule I can point to. You still have options, such as writing to the landlord again, reporting the noise to the police or the city, or ending the lease. Ending the lease is hard to support without a lease promise.

Do you want to stay in the apartment, or are you thinking of moving out over this?

DETAILS

### Does the law make the landlord act on a neighbor's noise?
- No. Each tenant must "Conduct himself or herself, and require other persons on the premises with his or her consent to conduct themselves, in a manner that does not unreasonably disturb the tenant’s neighbors or constitute a breach of the peace." (83.52(7)). That duty is on the upstairs tenants.
- The landlord can act against its own tenant. "If the tenant materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement… or reasonable rules or regulations, the landlord may:" send a notice (83.56(2)). The list of what gets no chance to fix includes "a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance." (83.56(2)(a)).
- That is a power, not a duty. Part II has no sentence that requires a landlord to act on one tenant's complaint about another.
- "Unreasonably" is not defined. You describe loud music most nights past midnight, and that goes beside the word. I can't say whether it meets the word.

### Does your lease add a promise?
- I read the whole lease. It has no clause about quiet, noise, quiet hours, other residents, or the landlord enforcing rules. It has no "quiet enjoyment" wording and no clause saying the landlord isn't responsible for other residents.
- So the lease makes no promise about other residents. Part II adds none. Whether other Florida law reads such a promise into a lease without words is outside this tool.
- Clause 10 says the lease is "the whole agreement" and changes must be in writing signed by both sides.

### Can you end the lease over this?
- Part II lets a tenant end a lease when the landlord fails a promise after a written 7-day notice (83.56(1)). That needs a promise the landlord broke.
- A neighbor's noise is not on the landlord's repair-duty list in 83.51(1). Local codes might cover it, but they aren't stored here.
- On the lease words I hold, that first condition is not met. Your letter of February 15 only asked the office to deal with the noise. It did not say you would end the lease, so it is not that notice.
- You've paid rent each month. That matters only if there were a landlord failure to give up. Whether paying rent with knowledge gives up the right is not settled, and I don't need to resolve it here.

### Can you sue the landlord for damages, or hold back rent?
- Damages under 83.55 also need a failure to meet the lease or part II. On the words I hold, there isn't one.
- Holding back rent is not a right here. The rent defense in 83.60(1)(b) covers only "a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1)". Stopping rent risks a written demand and an eviction suit.
- If you were sued, you would have 5 days, not counting Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after being served to pay the rent into the court or file a motion about the amount. Missing that is "an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)).

### What can you do now?
- **Write to the landlord again.** Part II sets no deadline for a reply. Give dates and times of the noise and ask what the landlord will do. Keep a log, any dated recordings, and every complaint and reply. This kind of letter only asks, so it does not end the lease.
- **Report it to the police or the city.** A report makes a record and may stop the noise. Local noise rules aren't stored here, so I can't say what they require.
- **Suing the upstairs tenants yourself.** Whether part II allows it is not settled. One reading says 83.52(7) is a duty in this part, enforceable by civil action under 83.54, and you are "the aggrieved party" under 83.55. The other says 83.55 covers only a landlord and a tenant under one agreement, and you have none with them.

### What if the landlord punishes you for complaining?
- Retaliation is unlawful. That includes raising your rent, cutting services, or threatening a suit "primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)).
- Whether an ordinary complaint about a neighbor counts is not settled. One reading says the listed examples are only examples, so a good-faith complaint can count. The other says the examples are all steps of a different kind.
- A landlord can't take your home without a court case (83.59(3)).
